Crucially, the World Bank Group Scorecard is proving essential not only in monitoring progress but in reinforcing institutional accountability.

Mobilizing private capital at scale remained a central priority for shareholders in fiscal 2026. Through targeted investments, advisory services, and robust risk mitigation instruments, the World Bank Group has helped crowd in private financing for infrastructure, agribusiness, manufacturing, and services — sectors that are indispensable for job creation. The Board welcomes the closing of the second securitization transaction under the IFC’s Emerging Markets Securitization Program, which demonstrates the viability of the institution’s originate-to-distribute model. BUSINESS OVERVIEW PRIVATE CAPITAL MOBILIZATION AND JOBS The World Bank Group is adapting to meet the scale of the jobs challenge, shifting from a provider of finance to a platform that channels global capital flows into developing countries. Rather than relying principally on our balance sheets, we are increasingly using financing, guarantees, data, and our convening role to crowd private capital into the most productive sectors for job creation. This means building investable pipelines, creating mechanisms that allow risk to be distributed across a broader set of investors, and connecting a much larger pool of global capital to development opportunities. In fiscal 2026, we made real progress and changes that are already translating into results. While financing from the World Bank Group’s own resources rose from $98 billion to $123.5 billion over the last five years, private capital mobilization surged from $35 billion in fiscal 2022 to $112 billion in fiscal 2026.

[wbg-ar-2026:p018:para1000:002 | wbg-ar-2026 | page 18]
This more than threefold increase represents a fundamental shift in our ability to bring external capital into development opportunities at scale, making us the largest mobilizer of private capital among multilateral development banks. Guarantees issued by the World Bank Group Guarantee Platform grew by 46 percent in fiscal 2026. We are providing patient equity in markets where early-stage capital is scarce and expanding local-currency financing where foreign-exchange risk would otherwise deter investment. We also began piloting “originate-to-distribute” approaches to connect institutional investors with emerging market assets at greater scale. And we’re providing investors and ratings agencies with historical data on the performance of emerging market lending through the Global Emerging Markets Risk Database. These practical shifts are already supporting investment and jobs.

question: How much faster does the World Bank Group now get projects approved?
answer: The World Bank Group cut average project-approval times from 19 months to nine, with some low-risk projects approved in as little as 60 days [wbg-ar-2026:p006:para1000:002].

• Knowledge transfer We’re applying our data and insights to better help clients create jobs. Assessments such as The Global Jobs Challenge map constraints, reforms, and investment opportunities. The World Bank Group Academy continues to build client capacity with practical, tested development solutions. • Greater efficiency Across the World Bank Group, we’ve consolidated country office leadership and eliminated bureaucratic duplication, making it faster and easier for us to address our clients’ priorities. We cut average project-approval times from 19 months to nine, with some low-risk projects approved in as little as 60 days.

[wbg-ar-2026:p005:para1000:001 | wbg-ar-2026 | page 5]
We changed how we work. We shortened average project preparation and approval times from 19 months to nine. We brought the institutions of the World Bank Group together around countries and clients — anchored in one country strategy built around each country’s needs and development priorities. We created a single platform for guarantees, simplified our products and internal structures, developed a purposeful work plan to support the private sector in emerging markets, and replaced a scorecard of 153 indicators with 22 measures focused on results. And we began building vehicles that can connect development projects with investors managing capital at real scale.

LETTER FROM THE PRESIDENT

Our Multiphase Programmatic Approach (MPA) enables countries to structure long, large, or complex engagements as a set of smaller, complementary Investment Project Financing and Program-for-Results operations within a single program. This approach facilitates both vertical programs, which involve in-depth, sustained engagement within a single country, and horizontal programs, which encompass multiple countries, states within a country, or subnational entities. In fiscal 2026, the World Bank approved 33 new programs totaling $25.1 billion in financing, comprising 15 vertical programs ($8.2 billion) and 18 horizontal programs ($16.9 billion). Total MPA project approvals comprised 95 projects totaling $17.7 billion, including nine additional financing projects totaling $1.0 billion. question: On current trajectories, how many jobs are developing countries expected to generate while 1.2 billion young people reach working age?
answer: On current trajectories, developing countries are expected to generate only about 420 million jobs while 1.2 billion young people reach working age over the next 10 to 15 years [wbg-ar-2026:p007:para1000:001].

events.query: 1.2 billion young people developing countries jobs

events.text: On current trajectories, developing countries are expected to generate only about 420 million jobs while 1.2 billion young people reach working age over the next 10 to 15 years [wbg-ar-2026:p007:para1000:001].

context:
[wbg-ar-2026:p007:para1000:001 | wbg-ar-2026 | page 7]
When we create jobs, we strengthen economic and social stability, reduce mass migration, improve livelihoods, enhance resilience to economic shocks, and prevent people from falling back into poverty. That benefits everyone, everywhere.

With 1.2 billion young people reaching working age in the next 10 to 15 years, the need for more and better-paid jobs is more urgent than ever. On current trajectories, developing countries are expected to generate only about 420 million jobs over that same period — leaving a gap of staggering proportions. Jobs are created when firms can operate reliably, plan with confidence, and invest with reasonable expectations of return. Our strategy reflects that reality:

• First, invest in foundational physical and human infrastructure;

• Second, support a business-enabling environment with clear rules and regulations;

• And third, mobilize private capital at scale.

[wbg-ar-2026:p005:para1000:000 | wbg-ar-2026 | page 5]
Ajay Banga

President of the World Bank Group Chairman of the Board of Executive Directors

JOBS ARE ESSENTIAL. THEY PROVIDE DIGNITY, HOPE, AND BELIEF IN A BETTER FUTURE. When jobs are created at scale, they strengthen communities, transform countries, and power the global economy.

Over the next 10 to 15 years, 1.2 billion young people will reach working age in developing countries. Those countries are expected to create only about 420 million jobs. Whether this generation becomes an engine of growth or a source of instability will depend in large part on whether they can find productive work.

That is why creating jobs is the overarching focus of the World Bank Group. Three years ago, our shareholders and clients gave us a clear mandate: build a better and bigger World Bank Group — faster, simpler, and better able to bring private capital alongside our own financing and knowledge.

[wbg-ar-2026:p032:para1000:003 | wbg-ar-2026 | page 32]
• 2.8 million students supported with better education. Over the past year, IFC continued to refine a new multi-year strategy to further scale its development impact. Our principal aim is to address the pressing need for jobs in countries where young people are entering the workforce faster than employment is being created. Built around four pillars — mobilizing private capital, expanding equity investments, revamping support for small- and medium-size businesses, and reinforcing coordination across the World Bank Group — we are strengthening our ability to support the businesses and entrepreneurs needed to create employment opportunities in developing countries. The business, operational, and thematic highlights that follow demonstrate how IFC’s evolving model is translating into concrete outcomes for clients, investors, and communities in the countries it serves.

question: What share of Jordan's domestic water supply is the Aqaba-Amman project expected to deliver by 2030?

Water security is foundational for productivity and economic growth. As one of the most water-scarce countries in the world, Jordan has struggled to grow its economy and create jobs for its young people. The government of Jordan is taking bold action to boost water security by initiating its largest-ever infrastructure project, the Aqaba-Amman Water Desalination and Conveyance Project. By 2030, the project is expected to deliver approximately 40 percent of Jordan’s domestic water supply. The project’s construction is directly creating 4,000 jobs and, indirectly, approximately 29,000 jobs, as well as advancing long-term job creation.

[wbg-ar-2026:p009:para1000:001 | wbg-ar-2026 | page 9]

IFC is also acting as an accredited entity for a $220 million concessional senior loan and a $75 million investment grant from the Green Climate Fund. For its part, MIGA received Board approval for guarantees of up to $1.25 billion.

Complementing the Aqaba-Amman project is IBRD’s $300 million Jordan Water Sector Efficiency Project, which includes financing from partners. This is strengthening Jordan’s broader water sector through non-revenue water reduction, energy efficiency, and distribution-system readiness. The World Bank Group’s support for Jordan’s water sector aligns with our Water Strategy Implementation Plan, which outlines how investments, long-term policy reforms, and institutional sustainability can deliver water security, economic growth, and job creation.

Our partnership with the government, launched in fiscal 2026, aims to support 1 million family farms with improved technology, market logistics, and insurance by 2030. This partnership is part of the World Bank Group’s strategic priority that aims to move 300 million farmers from subsistence to surplus. Our three-pillar strategy leverages the World Bank Group’s unique capabilities. First, the World Bank and IFC strengthen the foundations of family farms by investing in physical and human capital, such as rural roads and research. Then, they align regulations, streamline standards, repurpose subsidies, and remove barriers to doing business. The World Bank’s Pacific Healthy Islands Transformation (PHIT) project, approved in fiscal 2026, is taking a new approach to improving the health of people across the region. The $239.5 million project covers Fiji, Kiribati, Tonga, and Tuvalu, and — through the Pacific Community — Naoero, Samoa, Solomon Islands, and Vanuatu. question: Which bodies were combined into the Independent Accountability Mechanism?
answer: The Inspection Panel, the Compliance Advisor Ombudsman, and the Dispute Resolution Service were combined into the single Independent Accountability Mechanism (IAM). [wbg-ar-2026:p023:para1000:000]

In fiscal 2026, the Boards of IBRD, IDA, IFC, and MIGA approved the integration of the Inspection Panel, the Compliance Advisor Ombudsman, and the Dispute Resolution Service into a single Independent Accountability Mechanism (IAM). The decision drew on more than a year of deliberation and was informed by the recommendations of a Task Force engaged by the Boards. During fiscal 2026, ICSID registered 60 new cases — 57 arbitrations under the ICSID Convention and three under the Additional Facility Rules — bringing the cumulative total to 1,118 registered cases as of June 30, 2026. On the mediation front, ICSID had received a total of seven requests under Mediation Rule 6 and Mediation Rule 5, with one proceeding administered as of fiscal 2026. The year also saw 83 proceedings concluded, marking the third consecutive fiscal year in which conclusions surpassed 80.

Of the arbitrations concluded in fiscal 2026, 63 percent were decided by a tribunal and 37 percent were settled or otherwise discontinued, broadly reflecting ICSID’s long-term trend of arbitration outcomes. Among disputes decided by tribunals in the past year, 37 percent of awards upheld claims in part or in full, 40 percent rejected all claims on the merits, 18 percent declined jurisdiction, and 5 percent of cases were dismissed for manifest lack of legal merit.

CASE MANAGEMENT AND DISPUTE RESOLUTION ICSID administers investment disputes arising from contracts, treaties, or laws when agreed upon by the parties involved. Disputes are decided by an arbitral tribunal or a conciliation commission, whose members are typically appointed by the parties from among international jurists worldwide. The Centre also offers mediation and fact-finding procedures, and provides administrative services for arbitrations conducted under UNCITRAL and other non-ICSID frameworks. Fiscal 2026 was a record year for ICSID. The Centre administered 363 cases — the highest in its history — up from 347 in fiscal 2025 and 341 in fiscal 2024. In fiscal 2026, ICSID published its first in-depth study on contract-based investment dispute resolution, drawing on an analysis of 175 cases registered under the ICSID Convention and Additional Facility. The background paper examines how contract-based dispute resolution has worked in practice at ICSID, serving as both an analytical guide and practical reference for investors, States, and State entities. Key findings show that contract-based arbitrations at ICSID are more time-efficient than the overall caseload, averaging 40 months from registration to conclusion compared to 47, and settle or discontinue at a higher rate, 43 percent versus 34 percent.
